title: Highly sensitive person test (HSP): am I an HSP? — cv.cm
description: Free highly sensitive person (HSP) test: rate 14 statements on noise, crowds, emotions and detail to get a score from 0 to 56 and what it means. Not a diagnosis. Answers stay in your browser.
lede: Do loud rooms wear you out? Do you notice small changes, and feel other people's moods? Rate 14 statements to see how sensitive you are, and how to look after yourself if the answer is very.
about: The psychologists Elaine Aron and Arthur Aron introduced the term highly sensitive person in the 1990s to describe people with high sensory processing sensitivity: they notice more and take in what they notice more deeply, so they can also get overwhelmed sooner. Aron estimated that 15–20% of people are highly sensitive; a 2018 study by Lionetti and colleagues put the most sensitive group nearer 30%.

High sensitivity is a personality trait, not a disorder. The statements here were written for cv.cm; this is not Aron's HSP Scale, and half of them describe low sensitivity so that simply agreeing with everything doesn't raise your score. Our score bands are a rough guide, not research cut-offs.

faq.q: What does it mean to be a highly sensitive person?
faq.a: You react more strongly to what's around you: noise, light, crowds, art and other people's feelings. That can make you perceptive and empathetic, and also quicker to tire in busy places.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low sensitivity, 19 to 37 is medium, and 38 or more is high.

faq.q: Is being an HSP the same as being introverted or anxious?
faq.a: No. Many highly sensitive people are introverted, but a good share are extroverted. Sensitivity is about how deeply you process things; anxiety is about worry and fear. If worry is what troubles you, try the GAD-7 anxiety check on this site.
No. It is a normal variation in temperament and isn't a medical diagnosis. If you feel overwhelmed most of the time or it stops you living your life, talk to a doctor or therapist.

items: Loud noises, strong smells or bright lights quickly get to me.
A noisy, crowded place rarely bothers me.
I often sense how others feel before they say anything.
I don't usually notice small changes in a room or in someone's mood.
After a busy day I need time alone to recover.
I can go from one demanding thing to the next without needing a break.
Art, music or a beautiful view can move me deeply.
I'm rarely moved much by films, music or art.
I get flustered when I have a lot to do in a short time.
I stay relaxed when someone is watching me work or I'm under time pressure.
I think deeply about things and turn them over for a long time.
Once something is over, I don't give it much more thought.
Violent or upsetting scenes in films stay with me.
Other people's bad moods don't really affect me.

low.name: Low sensitivity (0–18)
low.body: You take noise, crowds and pressure in your stride and rarely feel overwhelmed. That's a real strength in busy settings. Remember that people around you may be feeling more than you notice.

mid.name: Medium sensitivity (19–37)
mid.body: You are sensitive to some things and not others, like many people. You probably notice when you need a break, and you can cope with a lively day. Pay attention to which situations drain you most.

high.name: High sensitivity (38–56)
high.body: You seem to notice and feel things deeply. That can bring empathy, care and a rich inner life, and also tire you faster. Protect some quiet time, build breaks into your day and don't treat your limits as a flaw.
